results.name: multiple_of_3_set_contrast
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples are all multiples of 3 (not all sharing a last digit), yes-rate for non-example targets that are multiples of 3 minus yes-rate for non-example targets that are not; observed above model means people generalise "multiples of 3" more sharply than the model's uniform-within-family multiples prior allows, below means less sharply.

results.name: power_of_two_target_yes_rate
results.description: Among sets whose examples are all powers of 2, the yes-rate for non-example targets that are themselves powers of 2 (e.g. 32 after "8,16", 8 after "64,4"); observed below model means people endorse the powers-of-2 concept less (the model's powers family prior / size principle is too strong), above means more.

results.name: shared_contained_digit_contrast
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all contain some common digit d but do NOT all end in the same digit, yes-rate for non-example targets containing d minus yes-rate for non-example targets not containing d; observed above model means people generalise "contains digit d" more than the model's (family-weighted) contained-digit rules allow, observed below means less.

results.name: cell_response_disagreement
results.description: Mean over (set, target) cells (each answered by several participants) of the within-cell response variance p(1-p); observed below the model mean means people agree with each other more (respond more deterministically) than the model's graded yes-probabilities imply, observed above means more disagreement than the model's probabilities imply.

results.name: inrange_narrow_minus_wide_span
results.description: Yes-rate on non-example targets lying inside [min,max] of the examples, for sets whose span is <=30 minus sets whose span is >=60; observed above model means people fill in narrow ranges more (relative to wide ones) than the Erlang interval-size prior predicts, below means wide ranges are filled in relatively more.
results.code:
# name: inrange_narrow_minus_wide_span
# description: Yes-rate on non-example targets lying inside [min,max] of the examples, for sets whose span is <=30 minus sets whose span is >=60; observed above model means people fill in narrow ranges more (relative to wide ones) than the Erlang interval-size prior predicts, below means wide ranges are filled in relatively more.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    parsed = {s: [int(x) for x in s.split(",")] for s in sets.unique()}
    lo = sets.map({s: min(v) for s, v in parsed.items()}).to_numpy()
    hi = sets.map({s: max(v) for s, v in parsed.items()}).to_numpy()
    n = sets.map({s: len(v) for s, v in parsed.items()}).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    inset = np.array([x in parsed[s] for s, x in zip(sets.to_numpy(), t)])
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    inside = (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~inset & (n >= 2)
    span = hi - lo
    a = r[inside & (span <= 30)]
    b = r[inside & (span >= 60)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: prime_set_contrast
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples are all prime, yes-rate for non-example odd prime targets minus yes-rate for non-example odd composite targets; observed above model means people generalise the primes concept more sharply than the model's family-weighted prime prior predicts, below means they treat primes like generic odd numbers more.

results.name: recency_nearest_example_contrast
results.description: Among non-example targets of sets with >=2 examples, yes-rate when the numerically nearest example is the LAST-shown one minus when it is the FIRST-shown one; the model is order-invariant, so observed above model means people weight recently shown examples more (recency), below means primacy.
results.code:
# name: recency_nearest_example_contrast
# description: Among non-example targets of sets with >=2 examples, yes-rate when the numerically nearest example is the LAST-shown one minus when it is the FIRST-shown one; the model is order-invariant, so observed above model means people weight recently shown examples more (recency), below means primacy.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    parsed = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in sets.unique()}
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    ss = sets.to_numpy()
    first = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    last = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    for s, ex in parsed.items():
        if len(ex) < 2:
            continue
        idx = np.where(ss == s)[0]
        dist = np.abs(t[idx][:, None] - ex[None, :])
        mn = dist.min(axis=1)
        nonmem = mn > 0
        uniq_near = (dist == mn[:, None]).sum(axis=1) == 1
        near = dist.argmin(axis=1)
        ok = nonmem & uniq_near
        first[idx[ok & (near == 0)]] = True
        last[idx[ok & (near == len(ex) - 1)]] = True
    if first.sum() == 0 or last.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[last].mean() - r[first].mean())

results.name: same_decade_contrast
results.description: Among non-example targets whose distance to the nearest example is 2-9, yes-rate when the target shares its tens digit with some example minus when it shares no example's tens digit; observed above model means people use decade (tens-digit) similarity beyond what the model's rules and intervals produce, below means less.
results.code:
# name: same_decade_contrast
# description: Among non-example targets whose distance to the nearest example is 2-9, yes-rate when the target shares its tens digit with some example minus when it shares no example's tens digit; observed above model means people use decade (tens-digit) similarity beyond what the model's rules and intervals produce, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    parsed = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in sets.unique()}
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    ss = sets.to_numpy()
    dec = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    mind = np.zeros(len(df))
    for s, ex in parsed.items():
        idx = np.where(ss == s)[0]
        tt = t[idx]
        mind[idx] = np.abs(tt[:, None] - ex[None, :]).min(axis=1)
        dec[idx] = ((tt[:, None] // 10) == (ex[None, :] // 10)).any(axis=1)
    sel = (mind >= 2) & (mind <= 9)
    a = r[sel & dec]
    b = r[sel & ~dec]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())
